title: Design a Web Crawler
brief: A search company wants to keep a copy of the public web fresh. The crawler is handed addresses to visit, must skip pages it has already seen, must not overload any single website, downloads each page, stores it, and pulls out the links that lead to more pages. If the memory of already-seen addresses is lost, the crawler must not turn that into a flood of duplicate downloads on other people's servers.
constraints: Accept and schedule about 4,000 addresses per second
About 45% of addresses are ones already seen, so even a perfect lookup removes no more than that
Every download passes a politeness limit so no site is overloaded
Pages come from the open web, which your plan limits to 5,000 requests per second
Stored pages go to cheap bulk storage; link extraction is helpful but optional
Old pages are refreshed by a background job

capabilities.label: Schedule the next addresses
capabilities.hint: Accept new addresses and decide the order to visit them

capabilities.label: Skip addresses already seen
capabilities.hint: Check whether an address was visited recently, using a fast lookup

capabilities.label: Limit the rate per website
capabilities.hint: Make sure no site is hit faster than it can bear. Applies to every address that is actually downloaded.

capabilities.label: Download a page
capabilities.hint: Fetch the page from the open web. Only addresses that were not duplicates get here.

capabilities.label: Save the page
capabilities.hint: Keep the downloaded page in bulk storage

capabilities.label: Extract links
capabilities.hint: Pull the links out of a page so new addresses can be found

capabilities.label: Refresh old pages
capabilities.hint: Revisit pages that have gone stale, about 300 per second

scenarios.title: Typical rate
scenarios.description: Steady scheduling at the usual rate.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Why does skipping duplicates early matter more than making downloads faster?
scenarios.debrief: Duplicates never reach the queue, so downloaders only handle new addresses.

scenarios.title: A huge seed list (2x)
scenarios.description: A big list of new addresses doubles the rate for a few minutes.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: Where does the extra work queue up, and what stops you exceeding the web plan's limit?
scenarios.debrief: The queue buffers the seed list and the downloaders autoscale, while the rate limiter keeps each site safe.

scenarios.title: The seen-address memory is lost
scenarios.description: The fast lookup that remembers visited addresses goes away.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: The duplicate check is gone. What happens to downloads and to other people's sites, and how do you defend them?
scenarios.debrief: The second replica keeps most of the lookup working. With one replica every duplicate would be downloaded.

scenarios.title: Download workers fail
scenarios.description: Whatever runs downloads loses an instance.
scenarios.interviewQuestion: A downloader dies mid-page. How do you avoid losing the address or fetching it twice?
scenarios.debrief: Another download worker takes the queued address, and the queue holds it until it is handled.

requirements.text: Addresses are accepted within the latency target at the usual rate
The design has a duplicate lookup, a queue, a politeness limit and bulk storage
Something downloads pages, politely, from the open web
Losing the duplicate lookup does not overload the web plan or the crawler
Losing a downloader does not stop the crawl
The design explains how a single website is protected

rubric: Addresses are deduplicated early with a fast lookup (a cache or a filter) before any work is queued.
Downloads are separated from scheduling by a queue, so slow websites do not block the frontier.
A politeness limit sits in front of the open web, per website, and is respected under bursts.
Pages and extracted links are handled by separate consumers; storage is cheap bulk storage.
Losing the duplicate lookup degrades gracefully (replicas, a persisted fallback) rather than flooding the web.

reference.summary: Drop duplicates before queuing, queue the work, download behind a politeness limit, and process pages in separate consumers.
design: Incoming addresses reach a Frontier Service running 'Schedule' and 'Skip addresses already seen'. The seen-address lookup is a Cache (2 replicas) in front of a Queue.
Download Workers (30 replicas, autoscale to 70) run 'Download a page' and the politeness limit through a Rate Limiter, then call a Third-party API standing for the open web.
Downloads feed a second Queue read by Store Workers (into Blob Storage) and Link Extraction Workers. A Refresh Worker revisits old pages.
tradeoffs: Deduplicating before queuing saves the most work, but a lost lookup floods the web plan, hence two replicas.
Cheap bulk storage keeps pages affordable but is slow to read back.
